$comment: What a deployment of this app has to provide, in a form a program can check.

This file is the contract #533 asked for. It is published three ways and they are the same bytes: it is in this repository at the tagged commit, it is copied into the image at /app/deploy/contract.json, and it is attached to the GitHub release for the tag. .github/workflows/publish.yml compares the copy inside the pushed image against this file before it creates the release, so 'the contract that came with this image' is a fact rather than a habit.

docs/publishing.md is the argument for every choice here. scripts/check-deploy-contract.mjs is what stops it drifting from the source it describes: CI fails if a variable is read and not declared, declared and not read, or if the port, the bind, the mount or the Postgres major written here disagree with the Dockerfile, the server or postgres-version.json.

Nothing site-specific is in here and nothing site-specific may be added: no domain, no hostname, no address, no credential. The consumer's own values go in the consumer's own repository. This says what the shapes are, not what the values are.

tagging.scheme: one immutable tag per release, spelled exactly as the git tag, e.g. v0.1.0
tagging.movingTags: none. There is no latest, no v0 and no v0.1. A moving tag would make 'what is running' unanswerable, which is the reason this publishes on a version at all.
tagging.why: A tag names a release for a person. A digest is the only thing that pins a build, so a consumer should deploy ghcr.io/blakehastings/book-scan@sha256:... and keep the tag in a comment beside it. Every release records its digest.

image.healthcheckNote: The image deliberately carries no HEALTHCHECK. GET /api/health answers 401 to anything without a session, so a probe has to treat 401 as healthy, and running one inside the container would cost a second Node process every interval. A consumer that wants a probe should write it knowing that. docs/the-image.md has the reasoning.

network.readThisFirst: The server listens on 127.0.0.1 inside the container, so publishing the port reaches nothing. `docker run -p 8080:3001` sets up a route to the container's own address and there is nothing listening there. This is the first thing a deployer hits and it does not look like a configuration mistake: the container is up, the log says it is listening, and every request from outside is refused at the socket.
network.whatTheConsumerMustDo: Put whatever fronts this app inside the container's own network namespace, so it can reach 127.0.0.1:3001 and be reached from outside. A tunnel daemon or a proxy as a sidecar sharing the namespace is the ordinary shape. Changing the bind is one line in this repository and is deliberately not made here, because what sits in front of it is the consumer's decision and is not knowable from this side.
network.sameOriginNote: One process serves the built client, the API and the photographs. The client addresses the API with same-origin relative paths and has no base-URL setting, so the client and /api must be one origin. Nothing has to route /api anywhere.

tls.why: The session cookie is set with Secure, always, in one place (web/server/auth/gate.ts). A browser will not store it over plain http on anything but localhost, so an origin that is not https and not localhost gives a sign-in that appears to succeed and lands back on the login screen. A phone will also not open a camera outside a secure context, which is what this app is for.

mounts.approximateSize: about 1.4 GB across roughly 1500 files, and it grows per book
mounts.whenMissing: Not an error. The image declares VOLUME ["/data"], so a container started with no mount gets an anonymous volume, writes photographs into it, serves them, and loses every one of them the next time the container is replaced. The names are in Postgres and the bytes are not, so what this looks like afterwards is an empty shelf rather than a failure.
mounts.backup: Must be backed up separately from Postgres and restored to the same moment. A database restored from one moment against a covers directory from another gives rows naming files that are not there, and the static mount answers 404 for each of them.

mounts.holds: the OCR models tesseract.js and ppu-paddle-ocr download on first use
mounts.whenMissing: Nothing is lost. A replaced container downloads a few megabytes again. A deployment that restarts often may want this mounted; it is deliberately not part of /data, because it is not data.

postgres.reachedBy: the ConnectionStrings__bookscan value, as a TCP connection from the container
postgres.why: postgres-version.json is the one place this major is written in this repository, and CI pins its own service container to it. Collation behaviour is a property of the server and the libc it was built against, so this is what the suite proves rather than a floor.
postgres.schema: applied by the container on every start, before it listens

outboundHttps.why: Identifying a book is what the app is for, and every source is an origin on the public internet. Without egress the app runs and identifies nothing.

signInHosts.for: signing in with Google: the authorization redirect a browser follows
signing in with Google: the token exchange, server to server
signing in with Microsoft: the discovery document, the authorization redirect and the token exchange, all three

outboundHttps.signInHostsNote: Listed apart from the five above because they are conditional and because they cannot be overridden: a provider's origin is not configurable, deliberately. Microsoft's is the trust anchor under an issuer this app does not otherwise know, so a variable that could move it would be a variable that could move who is trusted. Without egress to the host of a configured provider, the app runs, everybody holding a session keeps working, and nobody new can sign in.

start.migrations: Every start applies the schema, inside openPostgres, before the server listens.
start.concurrency: Migration is wrapped in a session-scoped Postgres advisory lock, so several containers starting at once is safe: one creates the schema and the rest wait and find it done. Driven with three containers against one empty database.
start.hazard: pg_advisory_lock waits without a timeout. A migration that hangs makes every other container's start hang behind it, which looks like a deployment that is up and never answers.
start.theLineToRead: `[db] postgres migrations: this database was empty, so the schema was created from them` is correct on a first start and is the finding on any start after that: it means the container opened an empty database that is not the catalogue, and it will come up reporting success with nothing in it.
saysOnEveryStart: which database it opened, host, port and name, never the credentials
whether a backup directory is watched
whether it is serving a built client
whether the development sign-in door is open or shut
start.notMultiProcessSafe: The advisory lock covers the schema and nothing else. The capture queue, the background crop worker and the cover downloader were written for one process. Two containers can safely start; that is not a claim that two should run.

stop.measured: docker stop --time 10 returns in about 0.24s, exit 0. Without the handler the same stop took the full 10s and exited 137, because the kernel discards a default-disposition signal sent to PID 1 and the image runs node as PID 1 in exec form.
stop.does: closes the listener, closes idle keep-alive connections, then closes the Postgres pool, which is what lets the process exit at all
stop.doesNot: A background crop or cover download that is mid-write when the signal arrives is cut off. Those writers do not write-then-rename, so a torn file is possible. The window is small and it is not zero.

refusals.result: the process exits 1 naming the variable

refusals.when: exactly one of BOOKSCAN_OIDC_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and BOOKSCAN_OIDC_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET is set
refusals.result: the process throws at start naming the one that is missing

refusals.when: any of BOOKSCAN_OIDC_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID, BOOKSCAN_OIDC_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET and BOOKSCAN_OIDC_MICROSOFT_TENANT is set and any of the three is not
refusals.result: the process throws at start naming the ones that are missing. Three rather than two, because Microsoft's issuer is scoped to a tenant and there is deliberately no default tenant.

the process throws at start. Those are authorities rather than tenants and have no single issuer: they sign in people from every tenant there is, and their own discovery documents say so by answering with the template https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantid}/v2.0 instead of a value. Accepting one would mean accepting any tenant, including one somebody registered this morning, which is an issuer check that proves nothing while sign-in still works. Name one tenant, by GUID or verified domain, or use "consumers" for personal Microsoft accounts.

refusals.when: a sign-in provider is configured and BOOKSCAN_PUBLIC_ORIGIN is empty
refusals.result: the process throws at start. Every OpenID Connect provider needs an absolute redirect URI and the server cannot build one without being told its own origin.

refusals.when: BOOKSCAN_DEV_SIGN_IN is set at the same time as a real provider is configured
refusals.result: the process throws at start. The development door signs in anybody who reaches it, so the two are refused together.

environment.name: ConnectionStrings__bookscan
environment.is: the Postgres connection string for the catalogue
environment.whenAbsent: The process exits 1 naming this variable. It is the only variable whose absence stops the server.
environment.note: This spelling and no other. Not DATABASE_URL, not PG*, deliberately, so an inherited shell variable cannot decide what gets written to.

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_DATA
environment.is: the directory the photographs live in; `covers` is joined onto it
environment.whenAbsent: Outside the image, the server resolves ./data against its working directory, creates it, and comes up reporting success while serving a catalogue whose every photograph is a 404. The image sets it to /data so that forgetting the mount costs an empty directory rather than a silent one in the wrong place.
environment.note: Overriding this points the app somewhere other than the declared mount. Do not, unless the mount moves with it.

environment.name: PORT
environment.is: the port the server listens on, on 127.0.0.1

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_BACKUP_DIR
environment.is: a directory the server watches for evidence that this catalogue has been backed up; read only, never created
environment.whenAbsent: Nothing is watched, and the start log says so. Empty means the same as unset, deliberately.

environment.name: GOOGLE_BOOKS_API_KEY
environment.is: the Google Books API key
environment.whenAbsent: A supported state. Requests go out anonymously into a shared quota that is permanently exhausted, so Google Books contributes nothing to identifying a book. /api/health reports whether a key is configured and never what it is.

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_OPENLIBRARY_URL
environment.is: the Open Library metadata origin

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_GOOGLE_BOOKS_URL
environment.is: the Google Books origin

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_COVERS_URL
environment.is: the Open Library cover image origin

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_LOC_SRU_URL
environment.is: the Library of Congress SRU endpoint

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_K10PLUS_SRU_URL
environment.is: the K10plus SRU endpoint

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_SRU_PACE_MS
environment.is: an override, in milliseconds, for the pace between requests to the SRU catalogues
environment.deployments: must not set this. It exists so a test run does not spend real seconds proving a rule about seconds; setting it low against the real catalogues asks them faster than they have agreed to be asked.

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_OIDC_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID
environment.is: the OAuth client id for signing in with Google
environment.whenAbsent: No real sign-in provider is configured, and the start log says so: nobody new can get in. Anyone already holding a session keeps it.

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_OIDC_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET
environment.is: the OAuth client secret for signing in with Google

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_OIDC_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID
environment.is: the OAuth client id for signing in with Microsoft
environment.whenAbsent: Microsoft is not a way in. Google, if configured, is unaffected.

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_OIDC_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET
environment.is: the OAuth client secret for signing in with Microsoft

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_OIDC_MICROSOFT_TENANT
environment.is: which Microsoft authority this deployment admits: a tenant GUID, a verified domain, or "consumers" for personal Microsoft accounts
environment.whenAbsent: Microsoft is not a way in. Set beside the other two, the process throws at start, because there is deliberately no default: Microsoft's issuer is scoped to a tenant and this app may not guess which authority a deployment is admitting.
environment.note: This is the second variable whose value is site-specific, after BOOKSCAN_PUBLIC_ORIGIN, and it must never appear in this repository. "common" and "organizations" are refused; see the microsoft-authority-with-no-issuer refusal above. Nothing else about Microsoft is configured or hard-coded: the issuer, the authorization endpoint and the token endpoint are read from https://login.microsoftonline.com/<this value>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration at the first sign-in, and docs/the-gate.md is the argument.

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_PUBLIC_ORIGIN
environment.is: the origin a browser reaches this app on, scheme and host, used to build the provider's redirect URI
environment.whenAbsent: Fine while no provider is configured. With one configured the process throws at start, because a redirect URI is an absolute URL and the server cannot invent its own origin.
environment.note: This is the one variable whose value is site-specific. Its value belongs to the consumer and must never appear in this repository.

environment.name: BOOKSCAN_DEV_SIGN_IN
environment.is: the subject a development-only door signs in as, which admits on sight
environment.deployments: must not set this. A deployment that sets it and configures no real provider has an account anybody who can reach it can sign into. Set beside a real provider the process refuses to start, which covers the configuration somebody would actually end up in; this covers the rest.

environment.name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
environment.is: an OTLP collector to export traces and metrics to
environment.whenAbsent: Telemetry is dormant and says so on start. Nothing is retried and nothing is logged.

environment.name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL
environment.is: grpc or http/protobuf
environment.whenAbsent: http/protobuf. Anything else is refused with a message and falls back to http/protobuf.

environment.name: OTEL_LOG_LEVEL
environment.is: how loudly the telemetry stack reports its own problems

environment.name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS
environment.readBy: the OpenTelemetry SDK, not this app's code
environment.is: headers sent to the collector, which is where a collector's credential would go

environment.name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
environment.readBy: the OpenTelemetry SDK, not this app's code
environment.is: the service name spans are filed under

firstUser.why: The gate admits nobody by default. A person who signs in for the first time lands on a waiting list, and the first user cannot be enabled by an enabled user because there is not one.
firstUser.runIn: the published image, e.g. docker run --rm <image> node dist-server/enable-user.js --target ... --enable ...
firstUser.note: Listing is the default and writes nothing. The target is taken on the command line and never from ConnectionStrings__bookscan, because this command writes and an ambient connection string must not decide what it writes to.

checkYourConfiguration.runIn: the published image, with the environment you intend to deploy with
checkYourConfiguration.does: Reads this contract from beside it and reports missing required variables, the four refusals above before the app hits them at runtime, unknown BOOKSCAN_ names that look like typos, and settings that are wrong for a deployment rather than merely unusual. Prints names and never values.
checkYourConfiguration.exit: 0 when there is nothing to fix, 1 when there is

notInThisContract: Any domain, hostname, address, network shape, tunnel credential or provider client id. Those belong to whoever deploys this and must never appear here.
A compose file, a chart, a wrangler.toml or any other descriptor that encodes topology. What runs beside this container is the consumer's decision.
TLS. Something in front terminates it.
Backups. The image cannot back up a mount it does not own.
